questions.q: What is adversarial training, as formalized in work like Madry et al. (2018)?
options: Training a model on adversarial examples, often generated with a strong attack like PGD, alongside clean data, so it learns to classify them correctly too
Encrypting a model's weights so an attacker cannot compute gradients
Removing all adversarial examples from a dataset before training begins
Training a completely separate model whose only job is to detect adversarial inputs and reject them outright
questions.explain: Adversarial training generates adversarial examples during training (commonly via PGD) and trains the model to classify them correctly alongside ordinary clean data.

questions.q: What did Tsipras et al. (2019) document about the robustness-accuracy tradeoff?
options: Adversarially robust models are always faster at inference than standard models
Adversarial training eliminates the need for a validation dataset
Adversarially robust models frequently show measurably lower accuracy on ordinary, unperturbed inputs than standard models
Robust accuracy and clean accuracy always improve together with no cost
questions.explain: The documented tradeoff is real: making a model more robust to adversarial perturbations often comes at the cost of reduced accuracy on normal, clean inputs.

questions.q: What did Carlini and Wagner's 2016 analysis show about defensive distillation?
options: It permanently solved adversarial vulnerability and is still the industry-standard defense today
It was later shown to mainly obscure gradients used by the specific attacks it was tested against, rather than making the model genuinely robust
It only works against malware classifiers, not image classifiers
It requires no additional training and can be applied to any model after deployment at zero cost
questions.explain: Defensive distillation initially defeated simple gradient-based attacks, but Carlini and Wagner showed a differently designed attack went straight through — it hadn't made the model truly robust.

questions.q: According to Athalye, Carlini, and Wagner's 'Obfuscated Gradients' work, what pattern did many proposed defenses share?
options: A technique that encrypts a model's output to prevent any inference at all
A method for compressing a model so it runs faster on edge devices
A formal guarantee that a model's prediction cannot change under any perturbation
A failure pattern where a defense appears robust only because it breaks the specific gradient-based attack used to test it, not because the real vulnerability is closed
questions.explain: Obfuscated gradients made gradient-based attacks fail without actually closing the underlying vulnerability; once attacks accounted for the obfuscation, the measured robustness collapsed.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of randomized smoothing (certified robustness)?
options: It removes the need to define a perturbation budget entirely
It guarantees robustness against every possible perturbation, with no limitations
It provides a certified robustness guarantee within a bounded perturbation radius, at the cost of extra compute from averaging over many noisy input copies
It works only on text classifiers, not on image or malware classifiers
questions.explain: Randomized smoothing provides a mathematically provable guarantee, but only within a bounded perturbation radius, and it requires significant extra compute per prediction.
